description:
We are Cultiva.io, a technology team that believes data from space can change the lives of people who work the land. In the Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data challenge, we are building a platform that turns NASA satellite data, such as soil moisture, rainfall, temperature and vegetation health, into simple alerts and recommendations for farmers: when to plant, when to irrigate and how to prepare for drought.

We combine software development, mobile apps and data analysis to help smallholder farmers adapt to climate change with information that is already public but still doesn't reach them. Our motto: "The field seen from space."
summary:
Cultiva.io is a free web platform that helps farmers choose the crop rotation that protects their soil and holds up against the climate ahead. Farmers mark their land on the map, tell us what they grow today and, in under a minute, see their current rotation side by side with three alternatives. Each option is compared on water security, soil health, income, resilience and soil loss.

To do this, we combine open NASA data (30 years of daily climate from POWER, soil moisture from SMAP, rainfall from GPM, vegetation from MODIS, groundwater from GRACE and terrain from SRTM) with NOAA's El Niño data, SoilGrids soil data and actual crop production figures from IBGE. We simulate each crop at 36 planting dates across all 30 years using the FAO water balance model. We estimate erosion with RUSLE.

This matters because the old planting calendar no longer holds. In Sorriso, Mato Grosso, the number of days above 35 °C a year rose from 55 to 93 in 20 years. The data farmers need to adapt already exists, but it isn't reaching them. Cultiva.io turns that data into plain farm language, with no sign-up, on any phone, in Portuguese and English.
details:
Cultiva.io answers the central question of the Field Shift challenge: which crop rotation will make my farm more resilient to a changing climate?

Farmers mark their land on the map (by GPS, by tapping, or by searching a place name). They choose their farm profile (smallholder/family farm, medium or large) and tell us what they currently grow each season.

The system then reads that location from open data sources:

  • NASA POWER: 30 years of daily rainfall and temperature;
  • NASA SMAP: current soil moisture;
  • NASA GPM IMERG: recent rainfall;
  • NASA MODIS: vegetation vigor (NDVI);
  • NASA GRACE: the trend in regional water storage;
  • NASA SRTM: terrain and slope;
  • NOAA: El Niño phase;
  • SoilGrids: soil properties;
  • IBGE: what the municipality actually harvests.

The engine simulates each of 21 crops at 36 planting dates in each of the 30 years. It uses the FAO-56 daily water balance and the FAO-33 yield response to water stress. That adds up to more than 20,000 simulated seasons per analysis. From them come the planting calendar, the yield potential in a typical year and the risk of crop failure.

The farmer's current rotation is compared with three alternatives, using the same data and the farmer's own priorities: water security, soil health, income and resilience. Soil loss is estimated month by month with the RUSLE equation, depending on whether the soil is covered or bare.

As the challenge asks, each alternative comes with five sections: why it was suggested, evidence (the data behind it), benefits, information gaps, and risks to review with an agronomist.

Real example: in Juazeiro do Norte, Ceará, the system confirmed that traditional corn with beans is the best of the rotations compared. It also showed that switching from common beans to cowpea eliminates the risk of crop failure on the best planting date and widens the planting window. And it warned that in El Niño years, the local rainy season had about 20% less rain.

Benefits

  • Decide before planting instead of counting losses afterwards: the right planting window, a safe date for the start of the rains, and the effect of El Niño measured on the farm itself.
  • Healthier soil: farmers see how many tonnes of soil per hectare the rain carries away, and how many months the soil stays bare, in their current rotation and in each alternative.
  • Estimated yields in kg/ha, calibrated against actual production in the municipality.
  • "What if the climate changes?" simulator: tests drought and heat scenarios and reruns every simulation instantly.
  • No barriers to access: free, no sign-up, works on a phone, shares the plan via WhatsApp, and available in Portuguese and English.

Intended impact
We want to bring satellite data that already exists, free of charge, to the people who need it most: small and medium farmers who still plant by a calendar from years ago. In Sorriso, Mato Grosso, for example, the number of days above 35 °C a year rose from 55 to 93 in 20 years. The goal is to reduce crop losses and erosion and to help farmers adapt to the climate. Extension agents and cooperatives can serve more farmers with a ready-made analysis that shows the source of every number.

Tools and technologies

  • Analysis engine: Python 3.12, FastAPI and NumPy (vectorized simulation of all dates and years at once).
  • Web application: Laravel (PHP 8.4), Blade, Alpine.js and Leaflet, as an installable app (PWA).
  • Database: PostgreSQL 17.
  • Infrastructure: Docker Compose, with a Caddy proxy for HTTP and HTTPS.
  • Data sources: NASA POWER, SMAP, GPM IMERG and GRACE (via NASA GIBS), MODIS (ORNL DAAC), SRTM, NOAA CPC, SoilGrids/ISRIC, IBGE SIDRA, Open-Meteo and OpenStreetMap.
  • Scientific methods: FAO-56 water balance and the WRSI index, FAO-33, RUSLE, Saxton & Rawls pedotransfer functions, and cross-validated regression.
  • Hardware: none. It runs on any standard server and on the farmer's phone.

Creative aspects

  • Starts from what the farmer already does: instead of prescribing a rotation, it compares the farmer's own rotation with alternatives and respects local knowledge. When the traditional rotation is already the best, the system says so.
  • El Niño measured, not assumed: instead of using a generic map, we classify each of the 30 years by ONI phase and compare rainfall and simulated harvests at the farm's exact location.
  • Linked rotations: the second crop starts when the first is harvested, and the first planting date is adjusted so the second crop still gets rain.
  • "The farm's story": four sentences that say where the land is, how it is doing today, what the best change would be, and what to expect this season.

Factors the team considered

Scientific honesty:

  • the yield model has a single climate parameter, so it doesn't memorize noise from just a few seasons;
  • climate is only added to the forecast when it beats the trend in out-of-sample validation;
  • model accuracy is published on the Transparency page.

Data limitations:

  • every number shows its source;
  • satellites measure averages over kilometer-wide areas, so the system accepts the farmer's own soil test;
  • every recommendation reminds the farmer to check it with an agronomist and against Brazil's official agricultural climate risk zoning (ZARC).

Field realities:

  • plain language, plus a glossary that explains terms with a tap;
  • works on slow connections and without a login;
  • if one data source fails, the analysis continues with the others.

Accessibility: calendar colors always come with a text label, and the interface is bilingual.
